newsitem.title: NEPAL: Survivor of Nepal avalanche tells harrowing tale.
newsitem.headline: Survivor of Nepal avalanche tells harrowing tale.

text.p: The leader of an American climbing expedition that lost two members in an avalanche in Nepal last week said on Tuesday he had to drink his own urine to stay alive.
"I diluted my warm urine with snow to drink," Cleve Armstrong, a 54-year-old doctor from Denver, Colorado, told Reuters after two days on a mountainside in driving snow.
"I could not eat much and used all my available energy to continually dig out the tent that was my life haven," he said.

Armstrong, who led the seven-member expedition to the 7,525-metre (24,690-ft) high Annapurna IV peak in west Nepal, was plucked to safety by an army helicopter on Sunday and brought to Kathmandu, the capital of the Himalayan kingdom.

Heavy snow had buried the expeditions' camp at 4,900 metres (16,050 feet) on October 4 and killed climbers Rich Davidson, 50, a computer engineer, and Debbie Marshall, 33, a forester, both also from Colorado.
"They had suffocated in their sleep...," Armstrong said.
The climbers' tent had a rear entrance with a zipper opening at the bottom, he said. If the pair had woken they were probably unable to unzip the tent after it was covered with about a metre of snow.
"Their feet were towards the vestibule so if they had become conscious when the tent collapsed they still could not have escaped...because one cannot crawl and claw feet first," Armstrong said.
Marshall, the mother of a 16-month-old boy, had wanted to be the first American woman to climb the Annapurna IV peak.
Armstrong struggled to keep alive in another tent six metres (25 feet) away.

"Huge avalanches were now raining down all around the camp, and I was beginning to feel like a mouse, kept alive and tormented by a cat for a long time before its death and consumption," he said in a statement.
When the snow stopped, Armstrong had to dig his way through a metre-high wall of snow before he could leave the tent.
Armstrong said the expedition was abandoned after he reported the tragedy to the Nepali government on Monday.
In another incident on a nearby peak, Japanese climber Masatsugu Konishi was reported missing after scaling the 8,163-metre (26,800-ft) Mount Manaslu, Nepal's Tourism Ministry said on Monday.
Annapurna IV is popular with Western climbers. October is the main month for expeditions.
Tourism, including royalties from climbers, is a key source of foreign exchange earnings for Nepal.
